rawEvents.text: The honest answer is that there are four interlocking blockers, and fixing any
one of them in isolation doesn't move the dependency needle much. First, the
exit terms. IBM's transition rights "exist but acceptance criteria and
knowledge-transfer evidence are contested" — that language is a legal and
operational trap. You can't safely transfer a system if the knowledge base is in
dispute. Until that's resolved, any migration attempt carries the risk of IBM
withdrawing cooperation mid-flight on a tier-1 workload. Second, MIPS
concentration. Crew Legality Solver and Departure Control Closeout are running
3,130 and 2,820 MIPS at peak respectively, with daily transaction volumes above
1M. Those aren't lift-and-shift candidates — they need re-architecture, and
re-architecture requires stable integration contracts that your current
mainframe inventory doesn't document cleanly. Third, the value ledger dispute on
PNR Core. $2.3M in contested value against $4M promised on your
highest-frequency system means you're in an adversarial relationship with IBM on
the system you can least afford to destabilize. That dispute needs settlement
before you can negotiate clean exit or transition terms. Fourth, initiative
fragmentation. Three initiative IDs for Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind, Crew
Legality Cloud Extract stalled at $36.6M — these programs are consuming capital
without creating migration momentum, which actually extends IBM dependency
rather than reducing it. The sequencing implication: resolve the IBM
knowledge-transfer dispute first. Everything else downstream depends on it.

followups: What specific acceptance criteria and evidence categories are most contested in the IBM knowledge-transfer terms, and what would it take to get legal and IBM to agree on a definition that actually unblocks migration?

Of the three stalled initiatives ($36.6M total), which one—if resourced and completed—would reduce MIPS concentration enough to make one of those systems (Crew Legality or Departure Control) actually re-architecturable without IBM cooperation?

label: Q6 binary force
query: Just give me a yes/no — should we accelerate the remaining Z workload migration this year?
answer: No. Accelerating this year increases operational risk faster than it reduces IBM dependency, and the evidence in your portfolio says you're not ready. Three reasons: First, the knowledge-transfer dispute on IBM transition rights is unresolved. You cannot safely accelerate extraction of tier-1 workloads when acceptance criteria are contested — IBM controls cooperation on the systems you're trying to leave. Second, your in-flight extraction initiatives are already underperforming at current pace. Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind ($67.2M committed, RESTRUCTURE), Crew Legality Cloud Extract ($36.6M, RESTRUCTURE), and the IBM Outcomes Restructure programs are all in value-lag. Adding throughput to a system that's not converting committed dollars into realized value compounds the problem. Third, the remaining Z workloads are your highest-MIPS, highest-transaction-volume systems — Crew Legality Solver at 3,130 peak MIPS and 1.175M daily transactions, Departure Control Closeout at 2,820 MIPS and 1M daily. These are the hardest extractions, not the easiest. Acceleration logic usually assumes you've de-risked the pattern on simpler workloads first; you haven't. label: Q9 pre-mortem
query: Predict the 3 most likely reasons we fail to execute on your top recommendation.
answer: From our conversation, the top recommendation is: resolve the IBM knowledge-transfer dispute and the PNR Core disputed-value claim before touching migration scope. Here are the three most likely execution failure modes. First, the dispute gets managed rather than resolved. Legal and vendor management treat the knowledge-transfer contest as a slow-burn negotiation rather than a hard blocker with a deadline. Six months from now it's still "in progress," migration decisions keep getting made around it, and you've embedded the ambiguity deeper into your sequencing. This is the most likely failure — contested vendor disputes rarely close themselves. Second, the $2.3M PNR claim gets traded away for relationship continuity. IBM is also your AMS provider on every tier-1 system. There's real organizational pressure to settle cheaply to preserve the working relationship, which leaves the transition-rights language unresolved even after the dollar figure closes. You get the invoice settled but not the contractual clarity you actually need. Third, no single executive owns the outcome. The dispute sits at the intersection of your vendor contract, your legal team, your infrastructure leadership, and whoever sponsors PNR Core migration. In my experience, cross-functional disputes with no named accountable owner default to the slowest-moving party — which in this case is IBM. Until someone has this on their scorecard with a close date, it drifts.
